recoveredSpeechGaps.transcript: The others came down the pasture at proper light, because Milo had woken and found two beds empty and a third man missing, and had got Weak up about it. There was a scene. Dessa had to say it four times, and Milo asked eleven questions, and Weak asked none. Senna, when she was told, up at the cart, with her hands folded on the blanket, said, well, obviously, which turned out to be the only piece of unmixed pleasure any of them got out of the hole.

Step, drag, stop. It went down the pasture in the gray before any color came into anything, and Torrin lay with his cheek on his arm and let it get about 40 yards away before he got up and followed it. He was not sneaking. He wanted that on the record afterward, at least with himself. He walked down the pasture in the open with his boots making their own noise on the same gravel. Rook heard him coming from a long way off, and turned his head, and did not send him back. Sit on that stone, Rook said. Don't talk. If you talk, I'll put you on the shafts for the day. Torrin sat on the stone. The bottom of the pasture flattened out into a strip of turf beside a beck about six feet wide and a hand deep, running fast and cold over pale stones. A line of alders stood along the far side. The sky behind them had gone the color of the inside of a shell, and there was mist on the water and nothing else moving anywhere in the world. Dessa stood on the turf with her weight on the good leg. Sit, Rook said. I've been sitting for ten days. Sit down, please. Not because of the leg. Because in about a quarter of an hour I'd rather you weren't standing when whatever happens happens. She sat down. Rook pushed his sleeve back, undid the strap, and took it off his arm. Torrin had never seen the underneath of it. The skin there was two shades paler than the rest of the forearm, and it had a permanent groove in it. A shallow trench worn by years of the same buckle at the same tension. And there was a white line across the outside edge where something had once gone through leather and skin together. The ember itself came away with a strap, held in a little pocket of stitched hide that had been repaired twice. He knelt down in front of Dessa and turned her left arm over. Tell me if this is too tight. It's fine. Tell me when it's too tight. Not whether it's fine. He set the oval against the inside of her forearm, two fingers below the wrist, exactly where Garruk had set Torrin's. And Torrin's stomach did something complicated at the sight of it. Rook took the strap in two holes further than he wore it himself. Now? That's right. Good. He sat back on his heels. I'm going to tell you four things and then I'm going to stop talking. And you're going to be on your own with it. And that's not me being difficult. It's that the fifth thing is the one nobody can hand you. All right? One. This is not going to work. That's not encouragement in reverse. It's the honest number. I have watched people try this about nine times in my life and I have seen it come off twice. And one of those two had been added for a year. He said it the way he read out a weight. Two. It is not going to hurt you. Nothing about this can burn you out or take anything from you. Because you have nothing in you to spend, which is the single piece of luck in your entire situation and I want you to have it. Three. He nodded at the thing on her arm. That is not a battery. Everybody thinks it's a battery. It isn't. It doesn't hold anything and it doesn't make anything. It's a handle on a door and the door isn't in the metal and it never was. Dessa said. Where is it then? That's the fourth thing and you're not going to like it. Rook stood up. It's in you. It's been in you since you were thirteen months old. Everybody's told you your door didn't open. What they meant, without knowing they meant it, is that the handle they gave you came off in your hand. He walked five paces away and sat down on the bank with his forearms on his knees. Go on then, he said. She tried for nine minutes and Torrin sat through every one of them. The first thing she did was what anybody would have done and what he himself had done in a rock cut on the worst morning of his life. She bore down on it. She put her right hand over the dark metal on her left arm and shut her eyes and went at it the way you go at a stuck jar lid, with her shoulders up around her ears and her whole face gathered into the middle. Nothing happened. Nothing kept happening for a long time. Right, Rook said at last, from the bank. Stop. Tell me what you were doing. Trying. Trying what, though? Say the actual thing. Not the word. Dessa opened her eyes. Wanting it. I was wanting it as hard as I could. I thought everybody says it happens when you want it. Everybody at my kindling kept saying, think about the thing you want most. And I did. And I've thought about it every day for a year and a bit. And I have wanted it more than anybody in that yard has ever wanted anything. I know. So what's left? Wanting isn't an instruction, Rook said. It's a weather. You've been standing in it for thirteen months. He got up and came four paces closer. Here's what actually happened just now, as far as I can see it from outside. You put your hand on a piece of metal and you ask the metal for something. The metal hasn't got it. I told you that five minutes ago and you nodded at me, and then you went and asked the metal anyway. Because everything you have ever been told in your life says the stone is where it lives. Then what do I ask? Nothing. That's the first half. He crouched. There's nothing to ask and nobody to ask it of. There's no one on the other side of that door handing things out. There is only a room you have been standing outside of because you were told the wrong thing about which side of it you were on. Dessa looked at him for a while. Well, that's not an instruction either, she said. No, Rook agreed. It's most of one. Try it again with the asking taken out. She tried it again with the asking taken out. And it was worse. Because now she had nothing to do with her hands. Torrin watched her sit very still for two minutes with her eyes shut and her palms open on her knees. And he watched her get frustrated. And he watched the frustration turn into the thing Dessa's frustration always turned into, which was accuracy. It's not working, she said. And I can tell you why, if you want it. I want it. I'm looking for something. She opened her eyes. Torrin told me about the warmth. Under the breastbone, about the size of a coin. He told me the day after and he's talked about it three times since without meaning to. And I've been lying in a cart for ten days going and putting my hand on that exact spot and finding out there's nothing there. Torrin's face went hot in the dark. So when you say stop asking, I stop asking, Dessa said. And then the only thing I've got left to do is go and look in the place where his is. And there isn't one. And that's the whole of every attempt I've ever made in my life. I go to the place. It's empty. I come back. Rook did not say anything for a moment. Right, he said. That's the best piece of information I've had in a fortnight. And I'm going to tell you something now that I was going to make you find on your own. Because you've earned not having to. He sat down on the turf in front of her. Properly. Cross-legged. Which Torrin had never once seen him do. There are two halves to this and I've given you the first one poorly. The first half is an empty head. Not calm. Not peaceful. Empty. Meaning you put down every single thing you have ever been told about where the power lives and what it looks like and who's allowed to have it. Including mine. Including his coin under his breastbone which is a true description of his and is not a map of you. He let that sit. You've been carrying somebody else's picture and going to somebody else's address. And the second half? Rook was quiet for a second. The second half is harder and it's got nothing to do with power. He said. You have to stop guarding. Dess's chin came up half an inch. Torrin saw it from twelve feet away. I'm not guarding anything. You're the most guarded person on that road. Rook said. Rook said. Without any weight on it at all. And you've got cause and I'm not going to stand here and tell you to put it down like it's a bad habit. Because it isn't one. It's a thing you built. And you built it for a reason and the reason was correct. You don't. You told me the reason yesterday afternoon in front of everybody. And then you sat down and let Wyke get a crate under you. He did not move. You see a thing. You say it out loud. Early. Correctly. And then somebody decides differently. And you do what you're told because that's what you agreed to. And it costs you. And it has cost you every single time. And once it costs you a leg. He paused. So somewhere in there you built a thing that makes that survivable. You hold the true thing out flat in your hand and you let people take it or not take it. And you never say I told you. And you never once let anybody see what it costs. That's the guard. It's a very good one. You're fourteen and it's already better than most grown peoples. Dessa's jaw worked. And you want me to take it down. For about a minute, Rook said. In a field, in the dark, in front of nobody but me and a boy who's going to keep his mouth shut for the rest of his life. Not forever. I'd never ask anybody that. Why does it matter? It's not. It's a feeling. What's a feeling got to do with a piece of metal? Because the door isn't in the metal, Rook said. I've told you that three times and you keep putting it down. The door's in you and a thing that is in you can be guarded against. And you have spent thirteen months getting extremely good at not letting anything out from in there where it might get looked at. He stood up. You've been doing the one thing that works. You just had it pointed the wrong way. He walked back to the bank. Empty head, he said. Nothing to find. Nowhere to go. Nobody to ask. And then don't hold anything shut. Torrin counted the seconds because there was nothing else to do with himself. At forty-one, Dessa's shoulders came down. He had not realized how far up they had been until they weren't. At sixty-eight, she stopped frowning. That was the thing he remembered. The frown went. And what was underneath it was not peace at all. It was a face he had seen once before. At a fire at Sallow Creek at somebody else's kindling. On a girl standing in a ring of people who were starting to talk about other things so she would have somewhere to look. At about ninety, her mouth opened slightly. At ninety-four, Torrin's ears popped. It was not a light. He went over it for years and he never got it any closer than that. There was no light on her and nothing came out of her. And the alders on the far bank did not throw a single new shadow. What happened was that for four seconds the dark got thinner. The mist over the beck. The gray turf. The shapes of the stones. The whole ordinary pre-dawn bottom of a sheep pasture. All of it got easier to see. The way the edges of everything had got easier to see at Torrin's own kindling with the fire in front of him. It did not get brighter. It got clearer. And it got clearer everywhere at once. Out to about fifteen feet. And the fifteen feet had Dessa Cole sitting in the middle of it with her palms open on her knees. The seam on the metal at her wrist opened. Torrin saw it happen and it made no sense to him at all. The dark oval came apart along a line it had no business having on somebody else's arm. And metal ran up over the back of her hand. Not fast. Nothing like the way it went for him. More like water finding the shape of a thing it was pouring over. And it went about three inches past her knuckles and stopped. It did not become anything. There was no blade and no hook and no strut. It was three inches of dull slate-colored metal lying across the back of a girl's hand. Unfinished. Stopped in the middle of an act. Like a word somebody had started and not needed to finish. Dessa made a small sound. Torrin counted four. On four the metal ran back down and closed. The dark came back in from fifteen feet and was ordinary again. The beck went on saying the same thing it had been saying all morning. Nobody moved. Then Rook got down off the bank onto one knee in front of her. And Torrin, who had been watching him for fifteen days the way you watch weather, understood with total clarity that he had not decided to do it. His legs had done it and the rest of him had arrived afterward. Don't speak yet, Rook said. He said it very quietly. Sit there. Don't move and don't try to do it again. Breathe for a bit. He put two fingers against the inside of her wrist, above the strap, and held them there. How's the leg? What? Your leg? Before anything else? Has it changed? No. It... No. She blinked at it. It hurts exactly the same. Good. That's what I wanted. He took his hand back. Now. Tell me what happened. I don't. You do. Tell me poorly. I'd rather have it poorly now than well in an hour. Dessa sat in the wet grass with her hands open. There was nothing in the way, she said. Rook did not move. Say it another way. I can't. Try. She looked past him at the water for a while. You know when you've been carrying something on a strap and you take it off? She said. And for about a minute afterward, your shoulder still thinks it's there. I've been walking around my whole life with the shoulder. And then for a second I didn't have the shoulder either. She frowned. That's worse. That's much worse than the first one. Give me one more. Why? Because I want three and then I'll stop. It was mine, Dessa said. She said it with some heat, which surprised all three of them. It wasn't a thing that happened to me. Nobody gave me it and I didn't find it anywhere. It was, it was already there. It was in the house the whole time. And I've spent a year standing on the step. She stopped. That's three. You said three? I did, Rook said and let go of her wrist. He did not write anything down. Torrin, watching from the stone, had the distinct impression of a man memorizing. How do you feel? Rook said. Fine. That's not an answer. It's a manner. Are you tired? Dessa opened her mouth to say yes. Because it was first light and she had been awake an hour and she had a broken leg. Then she stopped. No, she said slowly. I'm not. I am. That's odd, isn't it? I'm not tired at all. Something went across Rook's face. It was small and it was fast. The same size as the thing that had crossed it at the top of a gully when she said don't. And the same size as the thing that had crossed it in a firelit dark when Torrin said five generations. Torrin had never once been able to read it. He could not read this one either. But he was closer to it than he had ever been. Twelve feet away on a stone in the gray. And he saw that whatever it was, it went through the man's whole face and not just the front of it. And that it took Rook a full second to get the door shut on it. Do it again, Rook said. She could not do it again. She tried for twenty minutes. She tried every way she could reconstruct and then every way she could invent. And then, at the end sitting in wet grass with her hair stuck to her forehead, she tried simply sitting still and waiting for it to come back the way you wait for a word. It did not come back. It was there, she said. I'm not making it up. I know it was there. Then why? Because you weren't doing it, Rook said. You stopped doing about nine things. And then there it was. And now you know what it feels like. Which means for the rest of your life a part of you is going to be reaching for it. And reaching is one of the nine things. He held his hand out and she gave him the strap back. That's the shape of this. That's always been the shape of it. When Milo finally got round to asking him what it meant, he said. It means she did a thing. That's all it means yet. And when Wyke said flatly, can the rest of us have a go then? He said, no. And then, after a pause that was about a second too long. Not this week. Then he walked down to the beck and stood in it. Torrin saw him do it. He walked off the turf and into six inches of fast cold water in his boots. And stood there, facing upstream, with his hands at his sides. For something between two and three minutes. There was nothing in the water. There was nothing upstream. He was not looking at anything. He came out, and his boots were full, and he walked up the pasture past all of them and said, Twelve miles today. And that was the last thing anybody got out of him before noon. Rook had them doing the down man drill again on the barn floor in the dark, with the ground uneven and a beam in the way. And Milo was slow on the legs for the third time running. Faster on that side, Milo. I'm trying, it's... I know. Stop a second. Rook came over. Look where your feet are. You're standing square to him. So when you lift, you've got to turn and carry. And turning with a weight is the slowest thing a body does. Stand across him. Like that. Now your hips are already pointed at where you're going and all you're doing is standing up. He stepped back. That's the whole of it. It's not strength and it isn't speed. It's that you've been paying for a turn you didn't need to buy. Again. Milo did it again. It was nearly twice as fast. Better, Rook said. That was right. The second grab was right as well. You took the trousers, not the boot. Boots come off. Remember you did that. Then he moved on to Wick. Torrin stood in the dark of a half-roofed barn with his hands empty and a strange feeling under his ribs. And could not work out what was wrong with him. Later, lying down, he got it. Fifteen days. Fifteen days of no and again and wrong and that's a shape. Don't go looking for a better one shouted once across a rock cut by somebody else entirely. Fifteen days of a man who corrected them forty times a day and had never once, not a single time, explained why a thing was wrong or told anybody what they had done right. Milo had asked why about ten different things in a fortnight and had been answered exactly none of them. Tonight, he had been answered without asking. Torrin lay on his back under a broken roof and turned it over and could not make it into anything. Nothing had happened. A man had explained how to pick somebody up off a floor. That was all it was.
